Title: DPEPO: Diverse Parallel Exploration Policy Optimization for LLM-based Agents

DPEPO: Diverse Parallel Exploration Policy Optimization
for LLM-based Agents
Junshuo Zhang1,2, Chengrui Huang1,2, Feng Guo1, Zihan Li1, Ke Shi1
Menghua Jiang2, Jiguo Yu1, Shuo Shang1 and Shen Gao1

Abstract
Large language model (LLM) agents that fol-
low the sequential “reason-then-act” paradigm
have achieved superior performance in many
complex tasks. However, these methods suf-
fer from limited exploration and incomplete
environmental understanding, as they interact
with only a single environment per step. In
this paper, we first introduce a novel paradigm
that enables an agent to interact with multiple
environments simultaneously and share cross-
trajectory experiences.
Building upon this
paradigm, we further propose Diverse Paral-
lel Exploration Policy Optimization (DPEPO),
a reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm that
encourages the agent to perform diverse paral-
lel exploration. There are two stages in DPEPO:
initial supervised fine-tuning (SFT) imparts ba-
sic parallel reasoning and action generation,
followed by reinforcement learning stage with
a hierarchical reward scheme. We design a par-
allel trajectory-level success reward and two
step-level rewards: Diverse Action Reward
and Diverse State Transition Reward, which
actively penalize behavioral redundancy and
promote broad exploration. Extensive experi-
ments on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld show
that DPEPO achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA)
success rates, while maintaining comparable
efficiency to strong sequential baselines.1

adopt the ReAct paradigm (Yao et al., 2023), where
the agent alternates between reasoning and act-
ing: it selects a single action, observes the envi-
ronmental feedback, and then uses that observation
to inform its next step. This “reason, then act”
framework has shown notable success in complex,
long-horizon tasks (Shridhar et al., 2021; Yao et al.,

Recent work (Richens
et al., 2025) demonstrates that a comprehensive un-
derstanding of the environment is crucial for effec-
tive and reliable agents. However, ReAct imposes a
fundamental limitation: at each step, the agent can
perform only one action and observe a single obser-
vation. This restricts the breadth of environmental
exploration and forces the agent to construct its un-
derstanding from a narrow, linear view. As a result,
agents often develop an incomplete and biased cog-
nition of the environment, leading to suboptimal
decisions and failures in complex tasks.
A straightforward approach to broaden explo-
ration is to sample multiple independent trajecto-
ries for the same task. However, this naive multi-
sampling strategy faces two critical shortcomings:
(1) Lack of diversity: Despite increased output en-
tropy, actions sampled across multiple trials tend to
converge to similar choices, failing to promote truly
diverse exploration and preventing the agent from

developing a comprehensive grasp of the environ-
ment. (2) Inefficiency and isolation: Experiences
from different trajectories are neither shared nor
leveraged, meaning the agent cannot learn from
cross-trajectory insights. Moreover, sampling mul-
tiple trials sequentially inflates token consump-
tion and running time, making the approach pro-
hibitively costly for practical deployment.
To overcome these limitations, we introduce par-
allel exploration, a paradigm in which an agent in-
teracts with multiple environments simultaneously.
This allows the agent to gather diverse observations
in parallel, share experiences across environments,
and build a more holistic understanding of the en-
vironment dynamics. Building on this exploration
paradigm, we propose Diverse Parallel Exploration
Policy Optimization (DPEPO), a novel reinforce-
ment learning framework that endows agents with
structured parallel exploration capabilities. After
an initial SFT phase to acquire basic parallel rea-
soning and action generation skills, the agent is
optimized via a hierarchical reward scheme that en-
courages diverse exploration at both the trajectory
and step levels. Specifically, we design a parallel
trajectory-level success reward and two novel step-
level rewards: Diverse Action Reward and Diverse
State Transition Reward, that actively penalize re-
dundant behaviors. These rewards are combined
through a group-relative advantage computation
to provide multi-granularity learning signals, en-
abling the agent to explore more broadly while stay-
ing focused on task completion. Extensive exper-
iments on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, demon-
strate that DPEPO achieves state-of-the-art success
rates across all task splits. Notably, our analysis
of trajectory length and token usage reveals that
DPEPO achieves efficiency comparable to strong
sequential baselines, despite its parallel nature.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
• We propose Diverse Parallel Exploration Policy
Optimization (DPEPO), a novel RL framework that
pioneers parallel exploration for agents to build
holistic environment cognition.
• We design a Parallel Trajectory-level Success
Reward to optimize task completion in concurrent
multi-environment settings.
• We propose Parallel Step-level Rewards (Diverse
Action & State Transition) to penalize redundancy
and foster distinct explorations.
• Extensive experiments on ALFWorld and Sci-
enceWorld show DPEPO achieves SOTA perfor-
mance in terms of success rates while maintain-
ing comparable efficiency with single exploration
methods.

Related Work
LLM as Autonomous Agents
LLMs are increas-
ingly being deployed as autonomous agents across
a wide range of domains, including code genera-
tion (Zhang et al., 2024), web navigation (Abuel-
saad et al., 2024), smart device control (Zhang and
Zhang, 2024; Gur et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025b; Ye
et al., 2025), external tool use (Gao et al., 2024; Shi
et al., 2024, 2025; Huang et al., 2025) and interac-
tive gaming (Shridhar et al., 2021; Yao et al., 2022;
Wang et al., 2022, 2023). Early LLM-based agents
typically relied on engineered prompting strategies
(Wei et al., 2022) to achieve strong performance,
such as ReAct (Yao et al., 2023) and Reflexion
(Shinn et al., 2023). Recent studies has shifted their
focus toward fine-tuning LLMs for agent-related
tasks using either SFT (Song et al., 2024; Xi et al.,
2024) or RL (Feng et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025),
aiming to develop agents with greater generaliza-
tion ability and robustness, ultimately resulting in
more efficient and resilient behaviors compared to
earlier prompt-based methods.
Reinforcement Learning for LLM-based Agents
Reinforcement learning has been recognized as a
foundational approach for enabling LLMs to oper-
ate as autonomous agents in complex environments.
Early work in this domain primarily employed PPO
(Schulman et al., 2017), which allowed agents to
learn diverse interactive tasks while avoiding the
need for expensive imitation data. With the emer-
gence of reinforcement learning with verifiable re-
ward (RLVR) (Guo et al., 2025; Lambert et al.,
2025) and group-based policy optimization (Shao
et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025; Kool et al., 2019;
Liu et al., 2025c), a series of studies have elimi-
nated complex reward model and critic model, in-
stead adopting rule-based reward signals: GiGPO
(Feng et al., 2025) proposes anchor state groups
to estimate the quality of specific steps; RLVMR
(Zhang et al., 2025) introduces meta-reasoning and
corresponding step-level rewards to address ineffi-
cient exploration; iStar (Liu et al., 2025a) estimates
step rewards via the LLM’s intrinsic implicit re-
wards. However, these methods remain constrained
by the sequential ReAct paradigm, which limits
their exploration space and maintains a narrow fo-

3.2
Parallel Exploration Capability Cold Start
We begin with an SFT-based cold start stage to
endow the agent with foundational skills for struc-
tured output and parallel exploration. For the SFT
training data, we introduce human prior knowl-
edge into its synthetic pipeline. The data synthesis
pipeline is two steps: (1) We first manually anno-
tated five ground-truth trajectories. Each trajectory
consists of multiple steps, with some key steps con-
taining two or more parallel exploration actions. (2)
Based on these trajectories, we employ DeepSeek-
V3.2 to annotate trajectories containing parallel
exploration behaviors. Finally, the agent is fine-
tuned on these annotated trajectories, learning to
imitate the parallel exploration patterns.
Next, we employ a reinforcement learning
method to train the LLM to perform better parallel
exploration actions by using dual-level rewards as
the training signal: trajectory-level and step-level.

4
Experimental Setup
4.1
Datasets
We train and evaluate the LLM-based agents on
two challenging benchmarks: ALFWorld (Shridhar
et al., 2021) and ScienceWorld (Wang et al., 2022).
ALFWorld is a text-based interactive environment
where agents perform everyday household tasks
through multi-step reasoning and interactions. It
presents goals like “put the pencil on the desk”,
requiring agents to explore simulated rooms based
on common sense. The environment is fully text-
based and only returns a reward signal upon final
success or failure. ScienceWorld is a simulated
benchmark designed to evaluate scientific agent’s
reasoning capabilities across diverse elementary
science topics. It includes tasks from 10 domains,
including electricity, life cycles, and chemical reac-
tions. Each task consists of multiple intermediate
sub-goals that agents must complete sequentially.
4.2
Baselines
For ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, we compare
our approach with a range of competitive base-
lines under the ReAct paradigm: (1) Closed-source
LLMs: GPT-4o (Hurst et al., 2024), DeepSeek-
V3 (Liu et al., 2024), and DeepSeek-R1 (Guo
et al., 2025), which show superior performance
on various natural language tasks.
(2) A se-
ries of RL methods: GRPO (Shao et al., 2024),
which performs advantage estimation over trajec-
tory groups; GiGPO (Feng et al., 2025), intro-
ducing step-level advantage through anchor state
grouping; RLVMR (Zhang et al., 2025), which pro-
poses meta-reasoning rewards to address inefficient
exploration; and SPEAR (Qin et al., 2025), leverag-
ing self-imitation and intrinsic rewards to improve
the exploration–exploitation balance.
4.3
Implementation Details
We conduct experiments on various model sizes
of Qwen2.5-Instruct (Yang et al., 2025b) and
Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025a). For cold start train-
ing, we annotate approximately 500 and 1,000 for
ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, respectively. For re-
inforcement learning stage, the number of training
sample is 500, the temperature for rollout is 0.4, the
rollout group size N is set to 8 for ALFWorld and
4 for ScienceWorld, with 1 epoch and a total of 125
training steps. The max step is 25, and the number
of parallel environments is 4. Full hyperparameter
details and prompts used for training are provided
in Appendix B and Appendix C.

Experimental Results
5.1
Overall Performance
Table 1 demonstrates the performance of DPEPO
and baselines on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld
datasets. As illustrated, closed-source LLMs ex-
hibit only limited performance: On ALFWorld,
DeepSeek-R1 achieves a success rate of 80.1%,
and on ScienceWorld, GPT-4o reaches 45.2%. Un-
der the ReACT paradigm, RL training yields sub-
stantial improvements: GRPO raises the average
success rate on ALFWorld to 72.0% for the 1.5B
model and 77.5% for the 7B model, demonstrat-
ing the effectiveness of rule-based success reward.
However, the coarse-grained nature of this re-
ward limits further performance gains. In contrast,
GiGPO, SPEAR and RLVMR address this issue by
incorporating step-level rewards that provide more
fine-grained optimization signals for intermediate
reasoning steps. Among these methods, RLVMR
achieves the strongest performance, with average
success rates of 91.6% on ALFWorld and 47.5% on
ScienceWorld. Despite the demonstrated effective-
ness of these RL methods, they remain constrained
by the ReAct paradigm, which restricts the breadth
of environmental exploration and forces the agent
to construct its understanding from a narrow, linear
view. Our proposed DPEPO addresses this limi-
tation through parallel exploration and diversity-
driven rewards, achieving the best results: 98.2%
on ALFWorld and 61.4% on ScienceWorld. It also
demonstrates strong generalization on unseen ALF-

5.2
Scaling Abilities of DPEPO
In this section, to demonstrate the scaling poten-
tial of DPEPO, we present its performance across
models with varying model sizes. As shown in Fig-
ure 3, DPEPO exhibits consistent performance im-
provements and higher efficiency as the model size
increases, underscoring its generalization and scal-
ing abilities. Moreover, on the ALFWorld bench-
mark, even our smallest DPEPO variant (based
on Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct) outperforms the strong
baseline RLVMR by 2.53% in success rate and
completes tasks in fewer steps. On the more chal-
lenging ScienceWorld benchmark, DPEPO further
achieves higher performance with competitive ef-
ficiency. This highlights that diverse parallel ex-
ploration enables more effective and efficient task
completion. More scaling experiments conducted
on Qwen3 series can be found in Appendix A.1.
5.3
Analysis of Environment Numbers
Furthermore, we analyze the impact of varying the
number K of parallel environments during infer-
ence. For this analysis, we evaluate on both seen
and unseen tasks in ALFWorld and report the av-
erage success rate. During DPEPO inference, we
introduce a limiting prompt that specifies the max-
imum number of parallel environments the agent
is allowed to explore; any trial that exceeds K is
treated as a failure. We use GiGPO with multiple
sampling as our baseline; in GiGPO, K denotes
the number of sampled trajectories.

Conclusion
In this work, we propose a novel parallel explo-
ration paradigm and reinforcement learning algo-
rithm to address the constrained exploration chal-
lenge inherent in ReACT paradigm. We first ex-
tend the ReACT framework to enable agents to
simultaneously explore multiple parallel environ-
ments. We then introduce Diverse Parallel Ex-
ploration Policy Optimization (DPEPO), a novel
diversity-driven policy gradient algorithm specifi-
cally designed for parallel agents. By incorporat-
ing fine-grained, step-level rewards into the par-
allel trajectory-level success reward, DPEPO en-
courages agents to perform more diverse explo-
ration in parallel environments. Empirical eval-
uations across all test splits on ALFWorld and
the more challenging ScienceWorld benchmarks
demonstrate that DPEPO achieves state-of-the-art
performance and high sample efficiency. Through
extensive experiments and analysis, we show that
the diverse parallel exploration behavior reinforced
by DPEPO leads to superior task performance,
higher efficiency, and more effective token usage.

Limitations
While DPEPO shows significant improvements
in performance and efficiency, it still faces chal-
lenges in real-world scenarios where parallel envi-
ronments are hard to build. However, we suggest a
possible solution: training agents to complete dif-
ferent tasks in parallel, which might help mitigate
this issue in real-world scenarios. We leave this
exploration for future work.
Ethical Considerations
In some real-world environments that may con-
tain biases, parallel exploration enables the agent
to gather more experience, which could lead it to
learn those biases, potentially resulting in unfair or
unsafe behavior. Therefore, before applying our
proposed method to real-world tasks, developers
should conduct thorough evaluations in their target
environments to ensure the agent acquires accu-
rate and objective knowledge and performs actions
safely and responsibly.

which yields fewer but higher-quality samples for
policy updates.
A.4
Reward Hacking Analysis
Although we do not explicitly penalize over-
exploration in the reward design, the inherent con-
text window imposes a practical constraint. Ex-
cessive exploration across too many environments
causes a rapid increase in context length, and ex-
ceeding the context limit is treated as task failure.
Additionally, exploring too many environments
leads to redundant actions and state transitions. In
this situation, the diversity-driven step-level reward
naturally penalizes this behavior, which help re-
duce unnecessary exploration. We further present
the training dynamics of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct to
substantiate above claim. As shown in Table 5, the
agent’s exploration behavior remains stable.

A.8
Applicability of DPEPO Analysis
Although parallelizing interactions remains diffi-
cult in embodied agent scenarios, our paradigm is
highly applicable to a wide range of dominant cur-
rent agent scenarios. (1) Code Generation: Agents
can compile and test code in isolated, parallel san-
boxes to rapidly verify correctness. (2) Tool Learn-
ing: Agents mastering multiple tools and APIs can
invoke them in parallel to support simultaneous
sub-task execution or efficient trial-and-error. (3)
GUI Agent: Web or desktop environments can be
instantiated simultaneously in multiple headless
browsers or virtual machines. (4) DeepResearch
Agent: Information seeking tasks naturally sup-
port parallel querying across diverse search engines
and document sources. We hope these examples
illustrate that, though challenges remain in real-
world embodied scenarios, our approach still offers
a practical and efficient solution for many impor-
tant agent tasks. We look forward to further explor-
ing how this paradigm might be adapted to broader
scenarios in future work.

Experimental Details
B.1
SFT Training Details
Datasets
For ALFWorld, we annotate 500 suc-
cessful trajectories from the training split. For Sci-
enceWorld, we adopt the same data partitioning
strategy as RLVMR, which defines three difficulty
levels: L0, L1, and L2. For training on L0 and L1,
we annotate 1,000 trajectories from the L1 training
set (used for both L0 and L1 training for simplicity).
Consequently, our model faces a more challenging
L0 evaluation compared to RLVMR, as it is trained
with fewer L0-specific examples. For L2, we anno-
tate 500 trajectories for training.
Experiment and Hyperparameters Details
All
our SFT experiments are conducted using the
OpenRLHF framework. Specifically, we employ
DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 with Adam optimizer offload-
ing enabled. The model is trained with a maxi-
mum sequence length of 8,192 tokens, a learning
rate of 5e-6, and bfloat16 mixed-precision, with
FlashAttention-2 enabled in all experiments. The
batch size is set to 4 for ALFWorld and 16 for
ScienceWorld.
B.2
RL Training Details
Datasets
For both ALFWorld and ScienceWorld,
we select 500 samples from the training set that
excludes SFT samples for RL training.
Experiment and Hyperparameters Details
All
RL experiments is conducted based on verl-agent
framework and Ray-based dirtributed parallel en-
vironment. The maximum prompt length is set to
10,240 tokens and the maximum response length
to 2,048 tokens, with each trajectory allowed up
to 25 environment steps. The final actor learning
rate is 1e-6, and we employ parallel trajectory-level
reward that awards +1 for task success. Repetition
penalties are applied consistently across both envi-
ronments, with coefficients of 0.8 for depth-level
action repetition and 0.95 for width-level action rep-
etition, depth-level transition repetition, and width-
level transition repetition. Notably, ScienceWorld


includes an additional penalty coefficient of 0.5 for
invalid actions, which is not used in ALFWorld.
Both environments run with a maximum of 4 par-
allel exploration trajectories during training. For
group-based reinforcement learning, ALFWorld
adopts a group size of 8 while ScienceWorld uses
a group size of 4; in both cases, 4 distinct groups
are sampled per rollout. The rollout temperature is
set to 0.4, and the mini-batch size is 32. All policy
updates are performed using LoRA, with the LoRA
rank and scaling factor are all set to 32.
B.3
Computation Details.
For parallel environments, we cap the maximum
CPU usage at 0.3. For training on ALFWorld and
ScienceWorld, experiments with Qwen2.5-1.5B
are conducted on 4×L40 GPUs, and those with
Qwen2.5-7B on 4×H20 GPUs.
Each model is
trained for 1 epoch (500 samples) with 125 iter-
ations.

C.1
Prompt Details for Training
System Prompt
System prompt is crucial for
prompt engineering. The LLM follows the instruc-
tions and assumes the role specified in the it, such
as translator, programmer, etc. Therefore, as illus-
trated in Figure 11, we have provided a detailed
description of the desired behaviors of the paral-
lel agent within the system prompt to facilitate its
parallel exploration and thereby accomplish the
task better. Specifically, similar to ReAct, paral-
lel agent is required to engage in reasoning before
making a decision. For example, it needs to con-
sider which actions can be executed in parallel to
gather more information and which environments
warrant further exploration. This reasoning process
must be enclosed within the <think></think>
tags. After reasoning, the agent can take actions.
Unlike ReAct, the parallel agent can interact with
multiple environments simultaneously. Thus, we
require it to specify environment-specific actions
within <parallel></parallel> tags, with each
individual action wrapped in <env_i><env> tags
to clearly indicate which environment the action
belongs to and to enable easier parsing of the ac-
tions.
Prompt for First Step
At the beginning of a
task, the agent has not yet interacted with the en-
vironment. The environment provides only initial
state information, a set of available actions, and
the task description. We organize this informa-
tion into a concise yet clear prompt (As shown in
Figure 12) to help the agent understand the initial
context. Additionally, for ALF-World, we do not
include explanations for the available actions. How-
ever, for the ScienceWorld dataset, which involves
combinations of actions and objects, we introduce
brief action descriptions to avoid excessive token
consumption.
Prompt for Intermediate Step
As the number of
parallel agent exploration steps increases, maintain-
ing the full history of interactions becomes costly
in terms of both memory and computation. To ad-
dress this, at step t, for information from steps 1
to t −2, we retain only the actions and their cor-
responding observations within {history_info}. In
contrast, for the immediate previous step t −1,
we preserve all of the parallel actions, observa-
tions, and executable actions within {last_history}.
The details of {history_info} and {last_history} are
presented in Figure 14 and Figure 15. With this
carefully designed prompt presented in Figure 13,
the context length is reduced while still retaining
sufficient information for the agent to perform its
task more effectively.
Exploration-limiting prompt
For experiments
that require controlling the number of parallel envi-
ronments, we designed a prompt to limit the max-
imum number of environments the model can ex-
plore. In this prompt, we specify the allowed num-
ber of environments using “env_num” and inform
the model that if it attempts to explore more than
this number, the entire task will be considered a
failure. In addition to this prompt-based restriction,
we also enforce behavioral constraints: if the model
tries to access an environment that is not permitted,
the entire task is immediately seen as failed.
Action-Explanation Prompt
Since the tasks in
ScienceWorld require actions to interact with ob-
jects and involves a large number of both actions
and objects, it is impractical to include all possible
object-action combinations in the limited context.
Therefore, we adopt the same prompt as RLVMR,
which provides only a list of executable actions
along with explanations of their specific details and
the objects they can interact with. This prompt is
illustrated in Figure 17.

C.2
Effectiveness of Designed Prompts
Token Budget Analysis
When tackling long-
horizon tasks, traditional methods typically append
all historical information and intermediate reason-
ing steps into a single context window. However,
as the number of steps increases, the context con-
tinuously expands. In this section, we evaluate the
effectiveness of our designed prompt in compress-
ing the context window. As illustrated in Figure 10,
our method can compress prompts that originally
contain at most 50,000 tokens down to at most
7,000 tokens, significantly reducing the token bud-
get while still maintaining the agent’s strong per-
formance.
Comparison of Context Management Strategies
GiGPO employs a similar prompting strategy, but
instead of retaining all historical information, it
only preserves the most recent few steps within
a limited context window. We evaluate GiGPO’s
performance with varying context window sizes,
as shown in Table 8. Although the context length
may be shorter, its performance does not improve
as the context window expands. Furthermore, once
the number of retained steps exceeds 16, the total
context length will surpasses the model’s maximum
sequence length, leading to truncation.
In contrast, our proposed prompting design not
only preserves more comprehensive historical in-
formation but also adheres to the token budget.
Furthermore, as demonstrated in Section 5.2 and
Section 5.5, under our prompting scheme, the per-
formance of our method consistently improves as
the number of environments increases, highlighting
its efficiency, robustness and scalability.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents that fol- low the sequential “reason-then-act” paradigm have achieved superior performance in many complex tasks. However, these methods suf- fer from limited exploration and incomplete environmental understanding, as they interact with only a single environment per step. In this paper, we first introduce a novel paradigm that enables an agent to interact with multiple environments simultaneously and share cross- trajectory experiences. Building upon this paradigm, we further propose Diverse Paral- lel Exploration Policy Optimization (DPEPO), a reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm that encourages the agent to perform diverse paral- lel exploration. There are two stages in DPEPO: initial supervised fine-tuning (SFT) imparts ba- sic parallel reasoning and action generation, followed by reinforcement learning stage with a hierarchical reward scheme. We design a par- allel trajectory-level success reward and two step-level rewards: Diverse Action Reward and Diverse State Transition Reward, which actively penalize behavioral redundancy and promote broad exploration. Extensive experi- ments on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld show that DPEPO achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) success rates, while maintaining comparable efficiency to strong sequential baselines.1
